html:
The Lokono, long called Arawak, are a people of the coastal lands of the Guianas, in today's Guyana, Suriname, French Guiana and eastern Venezuela. Their language gave its name to the large Arawakan family, which also includes the language of the Taíno of the islands.

They farmed manioc on the sandy coast and along the rivers, fished, and traded widely by canoe. Their neighbours and rivals were the Kalina, a Carib-speaking people, and the Warao of the Orinoco delta.

They met Spanish traders from Trinidad early in the 1500s, and later became partners of the Dutch, who built plantation colonies in the Guianas in the 1600s, and sometimes caught runaway enslaved Africans for them. Today Lokono communities live in Guyana and Suriname, and a few thousand still speak the language.
